page: Amazon Web Services c8ine.large is a compute-optimized instance based on the AWS Nitro System architecture. It is powered by an x86_64 Intel processor operating at a clock frequency of 3.9 GHz. The instance provisions 2 dedicated vCPUs distributed across 1 physical core with 2 threads per core, accompanied by 4.0 GB of system memory, establishing a 1:2 vCPU-to-RAM ratio of 2.0 GB per vCPU.

The instance does not include local disk storage, requiring external networked block storage for operating system and persistent data needs. It contains no discrete GPU hardware. Network connectivity delivers a baseline bandwidth of 3 Gbps, and no complimentary public IPv4 addresses are assigned to the instance.

From a cost-efficiency and performance standpoint, the instance delivers dedicated, high-clock compute cycles without the risk of shared-resource throttling. However, the limited memory allocation of 4.0 GB and reliance on network-attached storage represent trade-offs that restrict memory-heavy or disk-intensive applications. It is suited for workloads prioritizing raw clock speed in a small footprint, such as microservices, web application tiers, CI/CD worker nodes, and lightweight batch processing.
description: Amazon Web Services c8ine.large is an eighth-generation compute-optimized instance built on the AWS Nitro hypervisor. It features an x86_64 Intel processor running at 3.9 GHz, delivering 2 dedicated vCPUs across 1 physical core alongside 4.0 GB of memory. Adhering to a compute-oriented 1:2 core-to-memory ratio, the configuration is tailored for workloads requiring dedicated processing power. The server contains no integrated local storage, requiring network-attached storage volumes, and does not incorporate GPU acceleration. Network performance is provisioned at a 3 Gbps baseline, with no complimentary public IPv4 addresses included. With constrained RAM and the absence of local disks, it is not structured for heavy in-memory data processing, but functions efficiently for lightweight compute-bound tasks, continuous integration runners, API endpoints, and batch processing workloads.
